title: What a saint is
hook: Paul calls every believer a saint; Catholics and Orthodox also honor holy people named by the church

segments.voice: Yesterday, agape: love that suffers long, written to a quarreling church. Your line was the greatest of these.

When you hear the word saint, what comes to mind? A stained-glass window, someone with a golden circle around their head. A city: San Francisco, Saint Louis, São Paulo. Or an eye-roll: well, I'm no saint. It means someone impossibly better than us. Now remember yesterday's church in Corinth: the fan clubs, the lawsuits, the rich eating first while the poor went hungry. How does Paul address his letter to them? To the church of God at Corinth, to them that are, as the King James puts it, called to be saints. That church. Those people. This week, the last of the stories, brings saints as real characters.
screen: `A GOLDEN CIRCLE, A CITY, AN EYE-ROLL.` → `I'M NO SAINT.` → `THE CORINTHIANS: CALLED TO BE SAINTS.`

segments.voice: The Greek word is hagios: holy, set apart, belonging to God. The Latin is sanctus, which gives us saint. In the New Testament it isn't a prize for the best people; it's a name for all of them. Paul opens his letter to Rome, in the King James Bible: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints." To Philippi: to all the saints in Christ Jesus. Every believer, in every messy church, holy not because they'd earned it, but because God had claimed them. Ordinary people, made holy. Over the centuries, Christians also began to honor particular people whose lives shone: martyrs first, then teachers, monks, mothers, people who gave their lives to the poor. The churches differ here. Catholics recognize saints through a formal process called canonization, and ask the saints in heaven to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Orthodox Christians honor saints in icons and hymns, and also ask their prayers. Anglicans and Lutherans keep calendars of saints' days and remember them as examples. Many other Protestants use the word mostly Paul's way, for every believer, and honor heroes of the faith without asking for their prayers. What all of them share is a line from the old creed: the communion of saints, God's people, living and dead, belonging together. The letter to the Hebrews pictures it as a stadium: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." And many churches keep All Saints' Day, November first, for the famous and the forgotten alike.
screen: `HAGIOS: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `PAUL: EVERY BELIEVER.` · `HOLY PEOPLE, HONORED DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `ORDINARY PEOPLE, MADE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Go back through your life and find one person whose plain goodness reached you: a teacher who noticed you, a neighbor who fed you, a grandparent; not famous, maybe not even religious. Picture their face, say their name quietly out loud, and let yourself be grateful. If you pray, you can thank God for them.
Saint. From the Latin sanctus, holy. In Paul's letters, every believer; in the churches' calendars, holy lives remembered.
Your line: ordinary people, made holy. Tomorrow, a mother who wouldn't stop crying for her son. Ninety days now.

Church positions summarized without ranking: Catholic (canonization, intercession), Orthodox (icons, hymns, intercession; glorification), Anglican and Lutheran (calendars; practice on invoking saints varies among Anglicans), many Protestants (all believers). Confirm each is fair.
Canonization history: the first papal canonization usually dated to Ulrich of Augsburg, 993; phrased as 'around the end of the first millennium'. Confirm.
All Saints' Day is November 1 in the West; Orthodox keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost. The script says 'many churches keep ... November first'.
